relationship_types.meaning: The source paper lists the cited paper (or an earlier version of the same work) in its reference list.
relationship_types.example: A 2015 paper whose reference list includes a 2009 paper CITES that 2009 paper.

relationship_types.direction: user of the method -> method (or the paper that introduced it)
relationship_types.meaning: The source paper applies a method. PAPER->PAPER form: the source applies a method that was introduced in the other (older) paper - as a component, baseline or tool - without necessarily changing it.
relationship_types.example: A paper that runs k-means clustering as a pre-processing step USES_METHOD the paper that introduced k-means.

relationship_types.direction: newer, extended work -> work being extended
relationship_types.meaning: The source proposes a new method by generalising, relaxing or modifying the other paper's method, and says so.
relationship_types.example: A paper proposing 'weighted k-means' as a modification of k-means EXTENDS the k-means paper.

relationship_types.direction: symmetric (order does not matter; stored with the smaller ID first)
relationship_types.meaning: Both papers' methods depend on the same underlying principle (named in the evidence), even if they use different vocabulary. A conceptual claim: you must name the principle and show it in both papers.
relationship_types.example: A GPS-positioning paper and an earthquake-location paper both locate a source by intersecting distance estimates (trilateration), so they SHARE_PRINCIPLE.

relationship_types.direction: symmetric (order does not matter; stored with the smaller ID first)
relationship_types.meaning: The problems the two papers solve have the same abstract structure (what is hidden, what is observed, what must be inferred), possibly in different settings or disciplines. An interpretation: it needs evidence that an author draws the analogy, or a clear mapping between the problem statements.
relationship_types.example: Locating a phone from cell-tower signal delays is ANALOGOUS_PROBLEM to locating an earthquake epicentre from seismograph arrival times; a paper that says so is evidence.

notes: Use participant IDs (P01, P02, ...) for source_id and target_id.
SHARES_PRINCIPLE and ANALOGOUS_PROBLEM are symmetric: P01-P02 and P02-P01 are the same edge.
CITES, USES_METHOD and EXTENDS are directed from the newer/using paper to the older/used paper.
Only assert a relationship you can point to evidence for. Wrong types count as wrong edges.
